props.title: 3 Women

sections.content: Three Women (1977) emerged from Robert Altman's actual dream, transforming into a haunting meditation on identity theft and personality absorption. The film follows Shelley Duvall's Millie and Sissy Spacek's Pinky in a sun-bleached California desert town, their relationship morphing from roommates to something far more psychologically complex. Like Altman's Nashville (1975), it weaves multiple perspectives, but here he ventures into territory closer to Persona (1966), exploring how identities can blur and merge.

sections.content: The film's dreamlike quality influenced a whole wave of identity-shifting cinema. Black Swan (2010) clearly draws from its DNA, while The Double Life of Veronique (1991) shares its interest in doppelgangers and merged consciousness. Altman's innovative use of water imagery and reflections created a visual language for psychological fragmentation that still influences filmmakers today. SUBHEAD: Desert Gothic and Female Identity

Altman transforms the Southwest setting into a character itself, much like how Paris, Texas (1984) would later use desert landscapes to externalize internal states. The swimming pool scenes, with their underwater murals by artist Bodhi Wind, create a dreamlike underworld that predates similar techniques in Under the Skin (2013). Shelley Duvall's performance as Millie - chattering endlessly to mask her isolation - ranks among cinema's great character studies.
